title: The One-Eyed Lion of Punjab
text: In 1801 the Sikh leader Ranjit Singh, only about twenty, was proclaimed Maharaja of Punjab in Lahore. Childhood smallpox had left him blind in one eye, yet he modernized his army, hiring European officers to train it. His kingdom stretched from the Khyber Pass to the Sutlej River, but it collapsed within about six years of his death.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Ranjit Singh (Khushwant Singh)

source2.name: Victoria and Albert Museum: Maharaja Ranjit Singh (painting, O114210)

title: Gia Long Stitches Vietnam Together
text: After decades of civil war, Nguyễn Ánh won decisive victories at Huế and Hanoi in 1802 and became Emperor Gia Long, ruling a reunited Vietnam from Huế. His court first asked Qing China to recognise the name Nam Việt. China refused, and after long negotiations the country officially took the name Việt Nam in 1804.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Gia Long

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: history of Vietnam (William S. Turley)

title: A European Court Moves to Rio
text: Fleeing Napoleon's invading army, Portugal's royal family and a horde of nobles and officials sailed across the Atlantic and landed in Brazil in 1808. Rio de Janeiro suddenly became the capital of a whole empire, the only time a colony served as the seat of government for its mother country. Rio soon gained a royal library, a botanical garden and a royal printing office.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Brazil: Independence

source2.name: Brown University Library, Five Centuries of Change in Brazil: Pedro I and Pedro II

title: Hidalgo Rings the Bell
text: Before dawn on September 16, 1810, the village priest Miguel Hidalgo rang his church bell in Dolores and called his parishioners to rise against Spanish rule. Thousands of farmers and workers joined him, starting Mexico's war of independence. Every year on the night of September 15, Mexico's president still rings that same bell and repeats the cry.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla

source2.name: UCLA Library, Frontera Collection blog: From Columbus to Hidalgo

title: Napoleon's Frozen Retreat
text: In 1812 Napoleon marched into Russia with the largest army Europe had ever seen. He reached Moscow in September, only to find it emptied and soon burning, with no one willing to surrender. Forced to retreat as winter closed in, he saw only about 112,000 of some 612,000 men return, and his army could never replace the trained men and horses it lost.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, French invasion of Russia

title: Shaka Takes the Zulu Throne
text: Around 1816 Shaka became chief of the Zulu, then a small chiefdom. He reorganized fighters into disciplined age-based regiments and armed them with short stabbing spears for close combat, instead of long spears thrown from a distance. By 1824 Shaka had no major rival in what is now KwaZulu-Natal, though his wars also brought huge upheaval to neighbors.

source.name: South African History Online, The Mfecane: Understanding a Period of Transformation in Southern Africa

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Shaka (Donald R. Morris)

title: San Martín Crosses the Andes
text: In early 1817 General José de San Martín led an army of thousands, plus mules and horses, from Argentina over icy Andes passes more than 3,000 meters high. It took about three weeks. Arriving in Chile by surprise, his army won the Battle of Chacabuco and freed Santiago from Spanish rule, a key step toward independence across South America.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Chacabuco

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, José de San Martín

title: A Trading Post Called Singapore
text: In 1819 Stamford Raffles of the British East India Company signed a deal with local Malay rulers to set up a trading post at the tip of the Malay Peninsula. He made it a free port open to all nations. The island then had about 1,000 people, mostly orang laut sea peoples, but by 1833 Chinese, Malays, Bugis, Indians and Arabs all lived and traded there.

source.name: National Library Board Singapore, Infopedia: 1819 Singapore Treaty

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Sir Stamford Raffles

title: Bolívar Wins at Boyacá Bridge
text: In 1819 Simón Bolívar did the unexpected: he marched his army across flooded plains and freezing Andes passes in the rainy season. On August 7 he caught Spanish royalist forces near a bridge over the Boyacá River, and the bulk of the royalist army surrendered. Three days later he entered Bogotá, and the victory led to the new republic of Gran Colombia.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Boyacá

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Simón Bolívar

title: A Prince Declares Brazil Free
text: On September 7, 1822, Prince Pedro, son of Portugal's king, proclaimed Brazil's independence on the plain of Ipiranga near São Paulo, and is remembered for crying "Independence or death!" On December 1 he was crowned Pedro I, Emperor of Brazil. Unusually, Brazil broke away from Portugal with a member of Portugal's own royal family as its new ruler.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Brazil: Independence

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Pedro I

title: Prince Diponegoro's Java War
text: In 1825 the Javanese prince Diponegoro rose against Dutch colonial rule after officials marked out a public road through his estate. Seen by many as a holy leader, he fought a guerrilla war for five years. In 1830 the Dutch invited him to peace talks, then arrested him and exiled him for life to Sulawesi.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Diponegoro

source2.name: UNESCO Memory of the World nomination, Babad Diponegoro (Indonesia/Netherlands)

title: Madagascar's Iron Queen
text: In 1828 Ranavalona I took the throne of the Merina kingdom after her husband's death and ruled Madagascar for 33 years. She pushed back hard against European influence, expelling missionaries and resisting British and French pressure. Her rule was harsh on Christians and opponents, so she is remembered both as a defender of independence and as a feared ruler.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Madagascar: Formation of the kingdom (1810-61), excerpted on its Ranavalona I page

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Africana (African Union project; Dictionary of African Biography), Queen Ranavalona I

title: Ram Mohan Roy's Long Campaign
text: For years the Bengali scholar Ram Mohan Roy campaigned against sati, the custom of a widow dying on her husband's funeral fire. In December 1829 the British governor banned it in Bengal. Roy, who read Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and English, also founded a reform movement and argued for women's property rights and modern schools.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ram Mohan Roy

source2.name: Women in World History (Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media, George Mason University), Sati: Official Documents, Regulation XVII of 1829

title: Emir Abdelkader Takes Command
text: In 1832, two years after France invaded Algeria, tribes near Mascara chose the young scholar Abdelkader to lead their resistance. He fought the French for some fifteen years before surrendering. Later, living in Damascus in 1860, he sheltered thousands of Christians during deadly riots, earning praise worldwide. A town in Iowa, Elkader, is named after him.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Abdelkader (Marcel Emerit)

source2.name: Grinnell College news, A Muslim Saint in Iowa

title: Slavery Ends in Jamaica, Slowly
text: On August 1, 1834, Britain's law abolishing slavery took effect in Jamaica and its other colonies. But freed people were forced into unpaid "apprenticeship" until full freedom came on August 1, 1838. Enslavers were paid £20 million in compensation while the formerly enslaved received nothing, a loan that, by one way of counting, British taxpayers were still paying off until 2015.

source.name: The National Archives (UK), The 1833 Abolition of Slavery Act and compensation claims

source2.name: UK Parliament, The West Indian colonies and emancipation

title: Ox Wagons on the Great Trek
text: From 1836, thousands of Dutch-speaking settlers called Voortrekkers loaded families into ox wagons and left Britain's Cape Colony, angry at British rule and the end of slavery. They pushed north and east into lands already home to the Ndebele, Zulu, Sotho and others. The journey led to new Boer republics and to years of conflict with African kingdoms.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Great Trek

source2.name: South African History Online, Great Trek 1835-1846

title: A Scholar Rebels for the Hungry
text: During the Tenpō famine, Ōshio Heihachirō, a former Osaka official and follower of Wang Yangming's Neo-Confucian philosophy, sold his library to help starving people. In 1837 he led an armed revolt against city officials and wealthy merchants. It was crushed in a single day, but the shogun's government was shocked that a former faithful official had rebelled.

source.name: Nippon.com, 'The Warnings of Famines Past' (Abe Haruki)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Japan: The maturity of Edo culture (excerpt on Ōshio Heihachirō page)

title: The Edict of the Rose Chamber
text: On November 3, 1839, the Ottoman government proclaimed a royal decree known as the Edict of Gülhane, or "Rose Chamber." It promised subjects of every religion security of life, property and honour, plus a standardized tax system. This began the Tanzimat, meaning "reorganization," decades of reforms meant to modernize the empire.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tanzimat

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mustafa Reşid Paşa

title: Hong Kong Becomes British
text: The First Opium War ended in 1842 with a treaty signed aboard a British warship near Nanjing. Qing China had to hand Hong Kong Island to Britain, open five ports to foreign trade and pay a huge sum in silver. Chinese writers later called it the first of the "unequal treaties," and Hong Kong stayed British until 1997.

source.name: MIT Visualizing Cultures, The First Unequal Treaty

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Nanjing

title: Ada Lovelace Writes a Program
text: In 1843 Ada Lovelace, daughter of the poet Lord Byron, translated an article about Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine and added her own notes, three times longer. One note set out step-by-step instructions for the machine to calculate special numbers, often called the first computer program. The machine was never built, but a programming language, Ada, is named after her.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ada Lovelace

source2.name: Computer History Museum, The Babbage Engine: A Brief History

title: The Potato Blight Strikes Ireland
text: In 1845 a water mold began rotting potato crops across Ireland, where the poorest third of the people depended almost entirely on potatoes. Over the next several years about one million people died and more than a million emigrated, mostly to North America. Even today, the island of Ireland has fewer people than its pre-famine population of about 8.5 million.

source.name: University College Cork, Atlas of the Great Irish Famine 1845-1852

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Great Famine

title: Liberia Declares Independence
text: On July 26, 1847, Liberia declared itself an independent republic, the first in Africa to do so. It had been founded by an American society as a home for freed Black Americans, and its first president, Joseph Jenkins Roberts, was born in Virginia. Its capital, Monrovia, is named after US President James Monroe.

source.name: Library of Congress, Teaching with the Library blog: Liberia, Africa's Oldest Independent and Democratic Republic

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Joseph Jenkins Roberts

title: A School for Girls in Pune
text: In 1848 Savitribai Phule and her husband Jyotirao opened a school for girls in Pune, at a time when most Indian girls never learned to read. Savitribai became one of India's first women teachers. People threw mud and dung at her on the way to class, so she carried a spare sari and kept going.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Savitribai Phule

title: The Black Ships Arrive
text: In July 1853, four American warships led by Commodore Matthew Perry appeared off Uraga, at the entrance to Edo Bay. Two were coal-burning steamships, and they entered under a cloud of black smoke; Japanese artists rushed to draw the "black ships." Perry demanded that Japan open to trade after about two centuries of tightly limited contact, and a treaty followed the next year.

source.name: US Department of State, Office of the Historian

source2.name: MIT Visualizing Cultures, Black Ships & Samurai (J. Dower)

title: India's First Passenger Train
text: On April 16, 1853, about 400 passengers in 14 carriages left Bori Bunder in Bombay for Thane, roughly 34 kilometres away, to a 21-gun salute, and the day was declared a public holiday. In the years that followed, railways spread rapidly across India, connecting people, goods and ideas faster than ever before.

source.name: Press Information Bureau, Government of India, 'From Steam to Speed' backgrounder (15 Apr 2026)

title: The Prophecy of Nongqawuse
text: In 1856 a Xhosa teenager named Nongqawuse said ancestors had told her that if people killed their cattle and threw away their grain, the dead would return and a whirlwind would sweep all white people into the sea. Many believed her, at a time of colonial pressure and a deadly cattle disease. Huge numbers of cattle were killed, and tens of thousands died in the famine that followed.

source.name: J. B. Peires, ''Soft' Believers and 'Hard' Unbelievers in the Xhosa Cattle-Killing', Journal of African History 27(3), 1986 (Cambridge)

source2.name: Journal of Natal and Zulu History 26 (2008), K. Breckenridge, 'Power without Knowledge'

title: Darwin Publishes His Big Idea
text: On November 24, 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, written at his country home, Down House. The first printing sold out to booksellers right away. It explained how living things change over time through natural selection, and fun fact: the word "evolution" does not appear in the first edition at all, though the very last word of the book is "evolved."

source.name: Darwin Online (John van Wyhe, ed.), R. B. Freeman introduction to On the Origin of Species

title: The Burning of the Garden of Gardens
text: In October 1860, near the end of the Second Opium War, British and French troops looted and then burned the Yuanmingyuan, the Qing emperors' vast garden palace outside Beijing. The fires took days to destroy its halls and gardens. Among the stolen treasures were twelve bronze zodiac animal heads, some of which have since come home to China.

source.name: MIT Visualizing Cultures, 'The Summer Palace of the Qing Emperors & its Destruction'

source2.name: MIT Visualizing Cultures, 'The Controversy Surrounding the 12 Zodiac Animal Heads'

title: Russia Frees Its Serfs
text: In 1861 Tsar Alexander II signed a decree freeing some 20 million serfs, peasants who had been tied to landowners' estates. It came two years before Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation in the US. The catch: freed peasants had to pay for their land through "redemption payments" planned to last 49 years, so many stayed poor.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Emancipation Manifesto'

source2.name: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Before Lincoln Issued the Emancipation Proclamation, This Russian Czar Freed 20 Million Serfs'

title: Two Minutes at Gettysburg
text: In November 1863, during the US Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln spoke at a new cemetery for soldiers killed at Gettysburg. The featured speaker before him talked for about two hours; Lincoln's speech was about 270 words and lasted roughly two minutes. It called for "a new birth of freedom" in a nation dedicated to the idea that all men are created equal, and became world-famous.

source.name: Library of Congress, Teaching with the LOC blog

source2.name: Library of Congress, Gettysburg Address exhibition

title: A Monk Counts His Peas
text: In the garden of his monastery in Brno, the monk Gregor Mendel grew and crossed thousands of pea plants, tracking traits like flower color and seed shape. In 1865 he presented the rules he found for how traits pass from parents to offspring. Almost nobody noticed until 1900, long after his death, when scientists rediscovered his work and founded genetics.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Gregor Mendel' (Robert Olby)

source2.name: Nature Education Scitable, 'Gregor Mendel and the Principles of Inheritance'

title: China Builds Its Own Arsenal
text: In 1865, as part of the Self-Strengthening Movement, Qing officials Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang developed the Jiangnan Arsenal in Shanghai to make modern arms, and in 1868 it built China's first modern steamship. Its translation bureau, led by the Englishman John Fryer, turned more than 160 foreign works into Chinese. The idea was to adopt Western technology without changing China's institutions or ideas.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Jiangnan Arsenal' (rev. Zhihou Xia)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Self-Strengthening Movement'

title: Canada Is Born
text: On July 1, 1867, the British colonies of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick joined to form the Dominion of Canada, with four provinces: Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Its capital was Ottawa, a former lumber town picked by Queen Victoria partly as a compromise between rival cities. July 1 is still celebrated as Canada Day, though Indigenous peoples had no seat at the table.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Confederation' (P.B. Waite et al.)

source2.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Ottawa'

title: Russia Takes Samarkand
text: In May 1868 Russian troops captured Samarkand, the old Silk Road city that Timur had made the greatest cultural centre of Central Asia. The defeated Emirate of Bukhara lost territory, paid an indemnity and was left at Russia's mercy. Samarkand soon gained a new section built after the Russian conquest, beside its medieval old city.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Central Asia vii. In the 18th-19th Centuries'

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Samarkand'

title: The Golden Spike
text: On May 10, 1869, workers drove a ceremonial golden spike at Promontory Summit, Utah, joining two railroads into the first line across the United States. Most of the workers who blasted the western section through the Sierra Nevada were Chinese immigrants. A trip from coast to coast shrank from months to days.

source.name: National Park Service, Golden Spike NHP, 'Chinese Labor and the Iron Road'

source2.name: Stanford Report, 'Giving voice to Chinese railroad workers' (2019)

title: An Empire Proclaimed in Versailles
text: On January 18, 1871, while Paris was under siege, King Wilhelm I of Prussia was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, in the palace of defeated France. Dozens of German states became one empire, which Germans saw as revenge for past French humiliations. In 1919 France's leader Clemenceau savoured his own revenge as Germany signed the treaty ending World War I in that same hall.

source.name: Palace of Versailles, 'Proclamation of the German Empire, 1871'

source2.name: Palace of Versailles, 'Hall of Mirrors'

title: A King Says Stand Up
text: In 1873, soon after his coronation, King Chulalongkorn of Siam issued a famous edict abolishing the custom of prostration, letting people bow instead. Over his long reign he also abolished slavery, reformed the courts and finances, and reorganized the government. By balancing the colonial powers against one another, he avoided colonial rule and left behind an independent kingdom.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chulalongkorn'

source2.name: Cambridge University Press, P. Jory, A History of Manners and Civility in Thailand, ch. 2 abstract

title: Zanzibar's Slave Market Closes
text: In June 1873, under a treaty with Britain, Sultan Barghash agreed to close all public slave markets in his lands, including Zanzibar's, the last permanent slave market in East Africa. A British missionary society bought the site, and an Anglican cathedral was later built on the very spot, with its high altar placed over the old whipping post.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Urban Heritage Atlas: Stone Town of Zanzibar

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tanzania: Zanzibar'

title: The Impressionists Are Named
text: In April 1874 a group of artists often snubbed by the official Paris Salon held their own show in a photographer's old studio. A critic mocked Claude Monet's hazy harbor painting, Impression, Sunrise, as a mere sketch or "impression," and the whole movement got its name. Some of the painters, a group including Berthe Morisot, later adopted the name themselves.

source.name: National Gallery of Art, '1874: The Birth of Impressionism'

source2.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline, 'Impressionism: Art and Modernity'

title: Tonga Writes a Constitution
text: In 1875 King George Tupou I gave Tonga a written constitution. Revised over the years, it is still in use today, one of the oldest written national constitutions in the world. During his long reign Tonga became a unified, independent kingdom with a legal code and modern government, though it later became a British protectorate from 1900 until 1970.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tonga: History'

source2.name: Matangi Tonga, 'Tonga's Constitution among the oldest in the world' (2014)

title: Mr. Watson, Come Here
text: On March 10, 1876, Alexander Graham Bell spoke into his new device in Boston and his assistant Thomas Watson heard him from another room: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you." Bell had filed his patent on February 14, just hours before a rival inventor, Elisha Gray, filed papers on a similar idea. Within years telephone wires crisscrossed cities.

source.name: Library of Congress Information Bulletin, 'Watson, Come Here' (April 2004)

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Alexander Graham Bell'

title: Korea's Doors Forced Open
text: In 1876 Japan, after sending gunboats to Korean waters, pressed Joseon into signing a treaty on Ganghwa Island. It opened Korean ports to Japanese trade and let Japanese citizens be tried by their own officials. Only about twenty years after American ships had forced Japan open, Japan was now doing the same to its neighbor.

source.name: Modern Asian Studies (Cambridge), 'Informal diplomacy in Choson Korea ... 1873-1876'

source2.name: Review of Korean Studies (Lee Keun-Gwan), 'Trope of a Sovereign State: Treaty-Making by Korea 1876-1899'

title: Egypt for the Egyptians
text: Colonel Ahmed Urabi led a movement against foreign control of Egypt under the slogan "Egypt for Egyptians." In July 1882 British warships bombarded Alexandria, and that September British troops defeated Urabi's army. Keen to safeguard the Suez Canal, Britain occupied Egypt and kept a strong grip on the country until after World War II.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, ʿUrābī Pasha

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Egypt: Renewed European intervention, 1879–82

title: Dividing Africa Around a Table
text: From November 1884 to February 1885, representatives of 14 countries, a dozen European states plus the United States and the Ottoman Empire, met in Berlin to settle rival claims in Africa. No Africans were invited. The conference sped up the "Scramble for Africa," and the Congo was recognized as the personal property of Belgium's King Leopold II.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Berlin West Africa Conference

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Leopold II

title: The Mahdi Takes Khartoum
text: In January 1885 the forces of Muhammad Ahmad, a religious leader called the Mahdi, captured Khartoum after a siege of more than ten months. British general Charles Gordon died in the fighting. A British relief force arrived just two days too late, and the Mahdist state went on to rule Sudan until 1898.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Siege of Khartoum

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Battle of Omdurman

title: Congress Meets in Bombay
text: In December 1885, 72 delegates from across British India met at a college in Bombay to found the Indian National Congress. One of its organizers was A. O. Hume, a retired British official. At first it asked politely for a bigger Indian voice in government; decades later, under leaders like Gandhi, it led the fight for independence.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Indian National Congress

source2.name: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Mumbai Legacy Project (D Ward): Badruddin Tyabji

title: The New Flower City
text: In the late 1880s Taytu, wife of the future Emperor Menelik II, persuaded him to move from cold Entoto, where firewood was scarce, to hot springs at the foot of the plateau. She named the new town Addis Ababa, meaning "new flower." As firewood ran short again, eucalyptus trees were imported from Australia in 1905 and spread to give the city forest cover.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Addis Ababa

title: The Yellow River Breaks Free
text: In September 1887 the Yellow River burst its levees near Kaifeng in Henan province and began flowing south into the Huai River. The flood covered thousands of square miles and buried many villages under silt. Estimates of the dead range from about 900,000 to two million, making it one of the deadliest floods in history.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Yellow River: Hydrology

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Huang He floods

title: Japan Gets a Constitution
text: On February 11, 1889, Emperor Meiji presented Japan's first constitution, modeled partly on Prussia's after officials toured Europe to study. It created an elected parliament called the Diet, which first met in 1890. Only a tiny share of men could vote at first, and the emperor kept enormous power.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Itō Hirobumi

source2.name: National Diet Library (Japan), Birth of the Constitution of Japan: text of the Meiji Constitution

title: Tragedy at Wounded Knee
text: On December 29, 1890, US soldiers surrounded a band of Lakota people at Wounded Knee Creek in South Dakota. Fighting broke out while troops were disarming them, and around 250 or more Lakota, many of them women and children, were killed. The massacre is often seen as the end of the long wars against Native nations on the Plains.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Wounded Knee Massacre

title: The Queen of Hawaiʻi Is Overthrown
text: On January 17, 1893, a group of mostly American businessmen, backed by US Marines, overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani of Hawaiʻi. She gave up power under protest to avoid bloodshed. Hawaiʻi was annexed by the US in 1898, and in 1993 the US Congress formally apologized. The queen was also a gifted songwriter who wrote "Aloha ʻOe."

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Sanford B. Dole

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Liliuokalani

title: Gandhi Thrown Off a Train
text: In June 1893 a young Indian lawyer named Mohandas Gandhi, holding a first-class ticket, was thrown off a train at Pietermaritzburg after a passenger objected to a "coloured" man in his compartment. He spent a freezing night in the station waiting room. He later called it a turning point that set him on the path of nonviolent protest.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mahatma Gandhi: Sojourn in England and return to India

source2.name: High Commission of India, Pretoria, Mahatma Gandhi in South Africa

title: The Donghak Peasants Rise
text: In 1894 Korean farmers, many following the Donghak or "Eastern Learning" religion, rose up against corruption and foreign encroachment and soon seized the provincial office at Jeonju. The Joseon court asked Qing China for troops, and Japan sent its own soldiers too. The rival armies clashed, setting off the First Sino-Japanese War.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Donghak Uprising

source2.name: Review of Korean Studies, Park Maeng-soo, 'Japan's "Distorted" Memory of the Donghak Peasant Uprising and the Sino-Japanese War'

title: Peace Talks at Shimonoseki
text: In April 1895 Qing China signed a treaty at Shimonoseki ending its war with Japan. China gave up Taiwan, recognized Korea's independence and paid a huge indemnity. During the talks, China's elderly envoy Li Hongzhang was shot in the face by a Japanese extremist; he survived, and the embarrassed Japanese side softened some terms.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Shimonoseki

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Li Hongzhang

title: The First Modern Olympics
text: In April 1896 the first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens, with track events in an ancient stadium restored in white marble. About 240 athletes from 14 nations took part, all men. The crowd went wild when Spyridon Louis, a Greek often described as a water carrier, won the brand-new marathon, which followed the legendary route of a messenger from Marathon to Athens.

source.name: International Olympic Committee (olympics.com), Athens 1896

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Athens 1896 Olympic Games

title: José Rizal's Last Poem
text: José Rizal, a doctor, novelist and speaker of many languages, wrote novels exposing abuses under Spanish rule in the Philippines. Accused of inspiring revolution, he was executed by firing squad in Manila on December 30, 1896. The night before, he wrote a farewell poem and hid it inside a small alcohol stove, which he left to his sister Trinidad.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, José Rizal

source2.name: Philippine Daily Inquirer: Haggling over the 'Ultimo Adios', by historian Ambeth Ocampo

title: The Curies Find Radium
text: In 1898 Marie and Pierre Curie announced two new elements found in the ore pitchblende: polonium, named after Marie's homeland Poland, and radium. Their July 1898 paper was the first to use the word "radioactivity." Their papers are still so radioactive that they are kept in lead-lined boxes, and readers must wear protective clothing and sign a waiver to consult them.

source.name: NobelPrize.org, Marie and Pierre Curie and the discovery of polonium and radium

source2.name: Christian Science Monitor: Marie Curie: Why her papers are still radioactive (2011)

title: The Hundred Days' Reform
text: In June 1898 the young Guangxu Emperor, advised by Kang Youwei, began issuing decrees to modernize schools, the army and government. After about 100 days, Empress Dowager Cixi seized power in a coup, imprisoned the emperor in his palace and had six reformers executed. A few moderate measures survived, such as new modern schools, including the university that became Peking University.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hundred Days of Reform

source2.name: Peking University News: Imperial University of Peking founded during the Hundred Days' Reform

title: Samori Touré's Last Stand
text: From 1883 Samori Touré, founder of a powerful Muslim kingdom in West Africa, fought French colonial armies, buying modern repeating rifles from traders in Freetown and setting up his own firearms industry. When pushed back, he tried to rebuild his state further east. He was finally captured in September 1898 and exiled to Gabon, where he died in 1900.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Samory

source2.name: Legassick, M. (1966) 'Firearms, Horses and Samorian Army Organization 1870-1898', Journal of African History (Cambridge)

title: Independence From a Balcony
text: On June 12, 1898, Emilio Aguinaldo's government proclaimed Philippine independence from Spain at his house in Kawit, as the new national flag was unfurled and a band played the national march. But months later Spain sold the islands to the US for $20 million. Filipinos then fought a bitter war against American rule.

title: The Boxers Rise in Shandong
text: After Yellow River floods devastated northern China in 1898, groups calling themselves the Righteous and Harmonious Fists spread through Shandong in 1899. Foreigners nicknamed them "Boxers" for their martial-arts rituals, which many believed made them immune to bullets. Angry at missionaries and foreign power, they marched on Beijing in 1900, where an eight-nation foreign army crushed them.

title: Mount Pelée Buries a City
text: On the morning of May 8, 1902, Mount Pelée on the Caribbean island of Martinique sent a glowing avalanche of hot gas and ash racing down onto the town of Saint-Pierre. It struck in less than a minute, and nearly all of the town's roughly 28,000 people died. One of only two known survivors, Louis-Auguste Cyparis, was shut in a prison dungeon and later toured with a circus.

title: The Herero and Nama Genocide
text: In 1904 the Herero people of German South West Africa rose against colonists who had seized their land and cattle. After a battle at Waterberg, German troops drove survivors into the Omaheke desert and later held many in deadly camps; the Nama people suffered too. Tens of thousands died, and Germany has since acknowledged it as genocide, sealed in a 2021 agreement with Namibia.

title: Exposing the Congo's Rubber Terror
place: Boma, Democratic Republic of the Congo
text: King Leopold II of Belgium ran the Congo Free State as his personal project, forcing villagers to collect wild rubber under brutal punishments. In 1904 British consul Roger Casement published a report based on his own trip upriver. Along with campaigns by missionaries and journalists, it helped build the pressure that led Belgium to take the colony away from Leopold in 1908.

title: China Ends the Imperial Exams
text: In 1905 the Qing government abolished the imperial examinations, which had chosen officials for about 1,300 years. Candidates wrote essays on Confucian classics in tiny cells that doubled as their bedrooms; Nanjing's Jiangnan Examination Hall alone had over 20,000 cells. The same year the court ordered new elementary schools and urged more students to study in Europe and America.

title: San Francisco Shakes and Burns
text: At 5:12 a.m. on April 18, 1906, a huge earthquake struck San Francisco, and fires burned for days, destroying more than 80 percent of the city's buildings. Around 3,000 people died. Because city records burned, many Chinese immigrants could claim they were born in San Francisco and bring over relatives, the so-called "paper sons."

title: Persia Gets a Parliament
text: In the summer of 1906, thousands of merchants, clerics and workers in Tehran camped in the garden of the British legation, refusing to leave until the shah agreed to reform. In August Mozaffar ad-Din Shah gave in and allowed a constitution and an elected parliament, the Majlis. The first Majlis met that October.

title: The Taste Called Umami
text: Chemist Kikunae Ikeda wondered why dashi, a broth made from kombu seaweed and one of his favorite dishes, tasted so good. He found the secret was glutamate and named its savory flavor umami, from the Japanese word for delicious. In 1908 he patented a way to make it as a seasoning, MSG, and soon a company called Ajinomoto was selling it.

title: The Bomb That Toppled an Empire
text: In October 1911 revolutionaries in Hankou accidentally set off a bomb they were building, and police found their membership lists. With nothing left to lose, soldiers in nearby Wuchang rose up on October 10. Province after province joined, and in February 1912 the boy emperor Puyi abdicated, ending China's 2,000-year-old imperial system.

title: First to the South Pole
text: On December 14, 1911, Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen and four companions became the first people to reach the South Pole. Their secret weapons were skis, sled dogs and reindeer-skin clothing sewn to a pattern from the Netsilik Inuit of the Arctic. They beat Robert Falcon Scott's British team by about five weeks, and Scott's party died on their return journey.
